migrationNotes: Spine: a teacher puts each class's own total beside every pupil, and the same idea of a window per group is followed from totals, to numbering that restarts, to equal-sized bands, to keeping one row from each group.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-partition-the-window-8 (numbering the last Y row) and -9 (why a customer's orders show one total). The second screen shows both. -5, -6 and -10 are the skill check.

lesson.title: Choose which rows a window sees

lead.text: In the last lesson the window was the whole table, put in some order. A window can be narrowed so that each row sees only some of the rows. PARTITION BY names the column that decides which rows belong together, and the rows that share a value in it form a window of their own. It goes inside the brackets after OVER, ahead of any ORDER BY.

Take the shop's orders and give each customer a window. SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) adds up the amounts inside the customer's own window and writes the answer beside every one of that customer's orders. Ada's two orders, 80 and 20, both show 100. Ben's both show 120. The window only gathers rows for the calculation, so every order keeps its own line, where GROUP BY would have merged them.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the windowed totals above the grouped ones. Cy's two orders both show 20, because the unknown amount on order 106 adds nothing to the sum. The grouped version gives the same three totals, but only one line for each customer.

queries.label: Totals beside the orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Totals as groups
queries.sql: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS customer_total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

lead.text: Work as the window does. Find the pupil's own class, then add up that class and no other.
Now partition by status instead. The paid orders form one window and the pending orders form another.

reveal.text: You added inside one window. The total repeats beside each of its orders.

queries.label: Group the report
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: Keep rows with status totals
queries.sql: SELECT id, status, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY status) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The numbering and ranking functions from the last lesson respect a partition too. Each window starts afresh, so a ROW_NUMBER with a partition begins at 1 in every group. Without the partition the numbers run on through the whole table.

Go back to the mark sheet and number the pupils from the highest score down. Over the whole sheet Bo (8) is numbered 1, Ann (6) is 2 and Cy (5) is 3. Partition by class and Cy's number changes, because Cy is the only pupil in class B and so comes first in that window. Ann and Bo are still numbered 2 and 1.

afterFigure.text: A number from a partitioned window says where the row stands among the rows of its own group, which is usually what a report is asking. The same holds for RANK and DENSE_RANK, and for every running calculation you meet later.

queries.label: One window for the whole sheet
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils ORDER BY position;

queries.label: A window for each class
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY class ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils ORDER BY class, position;

lead.text: Each customer's orders are numbered from the lowest id upwards, starting afresh for every customer.

reveal.text: You followed the numbering into one customer's window. It restarts where a new customer begins.

queries.label: One global window
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: One window per customer
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A window can also be cut into bands of equal size, such as the better and the worse half of a class. NTILE(n) does this. It lines the rows up in the stated order and deals them into n buckets, numbered from 1, so that no two buckets differ in size by more than one row. When the rows don't divide evenly, the first buckets are the larger ones.

Ten rows in four buckets show how the extras are placed. Four buckets of two use up eight rows and leave two extras. The extras go to the first two buckets, so the sizes are 3, 3, 2 and 2. Which bucket a row lands in depends on its position in the order, so rows with the same score can end up in different buckets. NTILE divides rows and takes no notice of how many different values there are.

afterFigure.text: The figure orders ten pupils by id and cuts them into four buckets, then into three. Use NTILE when a report needs groups of roughly equal size, such as the top quarter of scorers. Like the other window functions it can be partitioned, which cuts each group on its own.

queries.label: Four buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, pupil, score, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM marks ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Three buckets
queries.sql: SELECT id, pupil, score, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM marks ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The shop's five orders with a known amount are dealt into three buckets, larger buckets first.

reveal.text: You shared rows out by position. Buckets divide rows, not different amounts.

queries.label: Split A
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Split B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The last job is to keep only some rows according to a window value, such as the first order of each customer, which is the row numbered 1 in a partitioned numbering. The obvious attempt is to write position = 1 in the WHERE clause of the same query.

That doesn't work, and the reason is the order in which a query is evaluated. WHERE decides which rows are kept before any window function is worked out, so the number doesn't exist yet when WHERE goes looking for it. The numbers appear in the SELECT list, which comes later.

afterFigure.text: The fix is to number the rows in an inner query and filter on the number in an outer one, as in the second query of the figure. The outer query sees the position as an ordinary column of the inner query's result, so WHERE position = 1 now has something to test. The figure keeps Bo for class A and Cy for class B.

queries.label: Every pupil numbered
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY class ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils ORDER BY class, position;

queries.label: The top pupil in each class
queries.sql: SELECT name, class, score FROM (SELECT name, class, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY class ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM pupils) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY class;

lead.text: The shop wants each customer's first order, which means keeping the rows numbered 1.

queries.label: Number all customer orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: First order per customer
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, position FROM (SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS position FROM orders) WHERE position = 1 ORDER BY id;

lesson.orientation: Calculate within each row's group and filter the resulting values.
lesson.reviewLabel: Choose which rows a window sees
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A teacher has a mark sheet for two classes. Class A has two pupils, who scored 6 and 8. Class B has one pupil, who scored 5. She wants every pupil's line to show the total for their own class, so that a parent reading one line can see how the class as a whole did.

Two quick fixes both fail. A single total for the whole sheet would put 19 on every line, which mixes the classes together. Collapsing each class into one line gives the right totals but loses the pupils, and the sheet is meant to keep a line for each pupil. What she needs is a total worked out inside each class and written beside every line in that class.

Last lesson's rankings treated the table as one group. This lesson splits it into groups first, so that each calculation starts afresh inside its own group. The same idea then carries on to numbering, and the lesson ends by picking out one row from each group.

intro.promise: By the end you'll make a calculation restart inside each group, and filter rows on the value it produces.

recap.keyIdea: PARTITION BY gives each group its own window. Calculations restart inside it, and filtering on the result needs an outer query.

blocks.text: You wrote a class total of 14, then restarted numbering at 1 for customer 2. A paid total of 200 sat beside each paid order, and five orders split into buckets of 2, 2 and 1.

recap.nextHook: A total beside each line covers the whole group. A bank statement asks for something different: each line shows the balance so far, a total of only the lines above it. The next lesson builds those running figures and reads the rows just before and after.

questions.prompt: With PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id, what ROW_NUMBER does order 103 get?
hints: Look only at customer 2's orders.
Number them in increasing id order.
Order 103 starts customer 2's id-ordered partition; numbering restarts there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 103 is customer 2's first order, so its position in that customer's window is 1.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Order 103 starts customer 2's window, so numbering restarts at 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is its position in one run over all orders. Partitioning restarts for each customer.
Look at customer 2's orders only, in id order. Where does order 103 fall?

questions.prompt: What total does SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY status) attach to every paid order?
hints: Sum only paid known amounts.
The window repeats that status total next to each paid order.
Evaluate 80 + 20 + 80 + 20 for the paid partition.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The paid amounts are 80, 20, 80 and 20, totalling 200.

questions.onCorrect: 200. The paid window adds its known amounts once and repeats the total on each paid order.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds both statuses. The paid window holds paid orders only.

questions.prompt: With NTILE(3) over five known-amount orders ordered by id, how many rows are in bucket 1?
hints: Make the three bucket sizes differ by at most one.
Put larger buckets before smaller ones.
Distribute five records across three buckets with larger buckets first and size differences at most one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five rows split into buckets of 2, 2 and 1; the first bucket contains two.

questions.onCorrect: 2. NTILE gives the larger bucket first, so five rows split as two, two and one.

misconceptions.feedback: Bucket sizes differ by at most one, and five rows cannot fill that bucket with this many.
The larger buckets come first, so the first bucket is not the smallest.

questions.prompt: You have numbered each customer's orders with ROW_NUMBER and want only the rows numbered 1. How do you filter to position = 1 in SQLite?
hints: The filter must see the calculated column.

acceptedIdeas: Use an outer query over the numbered result
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compute ROW_NUMBER in an inner query or CTE, then filter position = 1 in the outer query. SQLite cannot use that window result in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.

choices.label: Use an outer query over the numbered result
Put the window function directly in the same query's WHERE

questions.onCorrect: Use an outer query over the numbered result. Then the filter can see the calculated column.

misconceptions.feedback: WHERE runs before the window value exists, so it cannot see it.
Renaming changes names, not the calculation.

questions.prompt: Seven rows are distributed by NTILE(3). How many rows are in the first bucket?
hints: Distribute rows as evenly as possible.
The larger bucket appears first.
Distribute seven records across three buckets, giving the first bucket the extra record.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three bucket sizes are 3, 2 and 2; the first bucket holds three.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Seven rows over three buckets give three, two and two, with the extra row first.

misconceptions.feedback: Sizes can differ by one, and the larger bucket comes first. Where does the extra row go?

hints: The calculation restarts independently within each partition.

acceptedIdeas: Which rows belong to each calculation window
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: PARTITION BY splits the rows into separate windows for the calculation. It changes which rows are compared or accumulated together without itself collapsing them.

choices.label: Which rows belong to each calculation window

questions.onCorrect: Which rows belong to each calculation window. The calculation restarts inside each partition.

misconceptions.feedback: Stored data never changes because of a query.
Keys belong to the table definition, not to a query.

questions.prompt: Class A pupils scored 6 and 8, and class B has one pupil who scored 5. Beside the pupil who scored 6 you write the total for their class. What do you write?
hints: Which pupils are in the same class as the one who scored 6?
Add up that class's scores.
Do not include the other class.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Class A scored 6 and 8, which total 14. That total goes beside each Class A pupil.

questions.onCorrect: 14. Each class has its own total, written beside every pupil in it. A partitioned window does the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds both classes. Each class has its own total.

questions.prompt: The rows are X, X, Y, Y, Y in id order. With ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY id), what number does the last Y row get?
hints: Numbering restarts for each group.
How many Y rows come up to and including the last one?
Count the Y rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Numbering restarts at the first Y row, so the three Y rows are numbered 1, 2 and 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. PARTITION BY gives each group its own window, so numbering restarts inside it.

misconceptions.feedback: That numbers all five rows in one run. PARTITION BY restarts for each group.

questions.prompt: Why does every order of one customer show the same total?
hints: Does the window keep the rows or merge them?

acceptedIdeas: The window total is repeated on each of its rows.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A window total is worked out once per customer and shown beside every row of that customer.

questions.onCorrect: The window calculates one total for the partition and repeats it on each row, keeping the rows.

choices.label: The window total is repeated on each of its rows.
The orders were merged into one row.
Every order has the same amount.

misconceptions.feedback: Windows keep every row. Merging is what GROUP BY does.
Amounts differ. The total is the same because it covers the whole partition.

questions.prompt: Group A has amounts 10 and 30. Group B has amount 5. What does SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY group) show beside the 10?
hints: Which rows share a window with the 10?
Only rows of the same group are added.
Add the group's amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 10 and the 30 share group A, so the total beside each is 40.

questions.onCorrect: 40. The window holds the group, so every row of A shows the group total.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the row's own amount. The window total adds the whole group.
That adds the other group as well. A window holds only its own group.
